questions.text: Plants and animals show variety in their forms and behaviour. This variety in nature is called
questions.explanation: Diversity refers to the variety of living things found in nature.

questions.text: A short plant with a soft, green stem is called
questions.explanation: Herbs are short plants with soft, green stems (e.g., tulsi, mint).

questions.text: A medium-sized plant with a hard, branching stem near the base is called
questions.explanation: Shrubs are medium plants with hard stems that branch close to the ground (e.g., rose, lemon).

questions.text: A tall plant with a thick, hard, woody stem is called
questions.explanation: Trees have thick, woody stems with branches high above the ground (e.g., neem, mango).

questions.text: Which plant is an example of a herb?
questions.explanation: Tulsi has a short, soft stem, making it a herb.

questions.text: Which plant is an example of a tree?
questions.explanation: Mango has a tall, woody stem, making it a tree.

questions.text: Leaves with veins that run side by side without a net pattern have
questions.explanation: Parallel venation describes leaves whose veins run side by side, like grass and maize.

questions.text: Leaves with veins forming a net are said to have
questions.explanation: Reticulate venation is the net-like vein pattern seen in mango and hibiscus leaves.

questions.text: Plants with parallel venation usually have
questions.explanation: Plants with parallel-veined leaves (grass, maize) typically have fibrous root systems.

questions.text: Plants with reticulate venation usually have
questions.explanation: Plants with net-veined leaves (mango, gram) typically have a taproot system.

questions.text: A seed that splits into two halves (cotyledons) is called
questions.explanation: A seed with two cotyledons is a dicot (e.g., gram, mango).

questions.text: A seed that has only one cotyledon is called
questions.explanation: A seed with one cotyledon is a monocot (e.g., maize, wheat).

questions.text: Animals that eat only plants are called
questions.explanation: Herbivores eat only plant matter (e.g., cow, deer).

questions.text: Animals that eat only other animals are called
questions.explanation: Carnivores feed on other animals (e.g., lion, tiger).

questions.text: Animals that eat both plants and animals are called
questions.explanation: Omnivores eat both plants and animals (e.g., humans, crows).

questions.text: A frog can live both on land and in water; such an animal is called
questions.explanation: Amphibians like frogs spend part of life on land and part in water.

questions.text: Fish breathe in water using
questions.explanation: Fish breathe through gills, which take oxygen from water.

questions.text: What is the MAIN reason scientists group plants and animals?
options: To make their study and identification easier
Because every species needs a number
questions.answer: To make their study and identification easier
questions.explanation: Grouping makes the huge variety of life easier to understand and study.

questions.text: Which is the BEST grouping criterion if you want to separate fish from frogs?
options: Whether they have gills only or both gills and lungs
questions.answer: Whether they have gills only or both gills and lungs
questions.explanation: Frogs have lungs (and breathe through skin) while fish only have gills.

questions.text: Which feature WOULD NOT be useful for grouping plants?
options: Number of friends the plant has
questions.answer: Number of friends the plant has
questions.explanation: Useful grouping features are physical features of the plant itself.

questions.text: You see a small plant with a soft, short stem. Which group does it most likely belong to?
questions.explanation: Short, soft stems are typical of herbs.

questions.text: Which animal group does a sparrow belong to?
questions.explanation: Sparrows have feathers, lay eggs, and have wings — features of birds.

questions.text: Why do animals living in cold places often have thick fur?
questions.explanation: Thick fur traps body heat and is an adaptation to cold environments.

questions.text: A camel can survive in a desert because it
options: stores fat in its hump that can be used for energy and water, and conserves water carefully
questions.answer: stores fat in its hump that can be used for energy and water, and conserves water carefully
questions.explanation: Camels are adapted to desert life with fat stores and water conservation.

questions.text: You are given two leaves: one with parallel venation and one with reticulate venation. The plants they came from MOST LIKELY differ in
questions.explanation: Parallel venation usually goes with fibrous roots and monocot seeds; reticulate with taproots and dicot seeds.

questions.text: Which of these is NOT a likely adaptation for an aquatic animal like a fish?
questions.explanation: Heavy fur is an adaptation for cold land animals, not for swimming in water.

questions.text: Why is biodiversity important to humans?
options: Many medicines, foods, and ecosystem services come from a wide variety of living things, and losing them makes life harder
questions.answer: Many medicines, foods, and ecosystem services come from a wide variety of living things, and losing them makes life harder
questions.explanation: Biodiversity supports food, medicine, clean air, water, and pollination — losing it harms human well-being.

questions.text: Cutting a forest reduces biodiversity mainly because
options: it removes the homes (habitats) of many plants and animals
it changes only the colour of the soil
questions.answer: it removes the homes (habitats) of many plants and animals
questions.explanation: A forest is a habitat for many species; removing it leaves them without home or food.

questions.text: While walking in a park, you find a plant with a tall, hard, woody stem; reticulate-veined leaves; and tap roots. It is most likely a
questions.explanation: Tall, woody stem with net-veined leaves and tap roots is the typical pattern for trees like mango.

questions.text: Which two animals are MOST likely grouped together based on the way they move?
options: A bird and a butterfly (both fly)
questions.answer: A bird and a butterfly (both fly)
questions.explanation: Birds and butterflies share flight as their mode of movement.

questions.text: Animals that lay eggs and have feathers are called
questions.explanation: Birds have feathers and lay eggs.

questions.text: Animals that have hair or fur and feed their young with milk are called
questions.explanation: Mammals have hair/fur and produce milk for their young.

questions.text: Mango is a tree.
questions.explanation: Mango has a tall, woody stem typical of trees.

questions.text: Tulsi is a tree.
questions.explanation: Tulsi is a herb because of its short, soft stem.

questions.text: All living things in a region together make up its biodiversity.
questions.explanation: Biodiversity is the total variety of life in a region.

questions.text: Grouping makes it easier to study and identify living things.
questions.explanation: Classification simplifies the study of life's huge variety.

questions.text: Maize seeds are dicots.
questions.explanation: Maize seeds are monocots (one cotyledon).

questions.text: Plants with reticulate venation usually have a fibrous root system.
questions.explanation: Reticulate venation is usually paired with a taproot system.

questions.text: Frogs are amphibians because they live both on land and in water.
questions.explanation: Amphibians like frogs are adapted to life in both land and water.

questions.text: All birds can fly.
questions.explanation: Some birds, like ostriches and penguins, cannot fly.

questions.text: A whale is a fish because it lives in the sea.
questions.explanation: Whales are mammals — they breathe air through lungs and feed milk to their young — not fish.

questions.text: If we lose a species, we can usually bring it back from another location easily.
questions.explanation: Once a species is extinct (or locally lost), recovery is rare and very hard, because every population is unique.

questions.text: Different students grouping the same set of animals must always use the same feature.
questions.explanation: Different valid groupings can use different features (food, habitat, movement).

questions.text: A short plant with a soft, green stem is called a _____.
questions.explanation: Herbs are short and have soft, green stems.

questions.text: A medium-sized plant with hard branching stems near the base is a _____.
questions.explanation: Shrubs are between herbs and trees in size.

questions.text: A tall plant with a thick, hard, woody stem is a _____.
questions.explanation: Trees have thick, woody stems and branches above the ground.

questions.text: Animals that eat only plants are called _____.
questions.explanation: Herbivores eat plants only.

questions.text: Animals that eat only other animals are called _____.
questions.explanation: Carnivores eat other animals.

questions.text: Animals that eat both plants and animals are called _____.
questions.explanation: Omnivores eat plants as well as animals.

questions.text: Fish breathe through _____.
questions.explanation: Gills let fish take oxygen from water.

questions.text: A leaf with veins forming a net-like pattern is said to have _____ venation.
questions.explanation: Reticulate venation is the net pattern.

questions.text: A leaf with veins running side by side without a net is said to have _____ venation.
questions.explanation: Parallel venation has veins running parallel.

questions.text: The total variety of plants, animals, and other living things in a particular area is called _____.
questions.explanation: Biodiversity = biological diversity in a region.

questions.text: A seed that splits into two halves is called a _____.
questions.explanation: Dicots have two cotyledons.

questions.text: A plant with parallel-veined leaves is most likely to have a _____ root system.
questions.explanation: Parallel venation usually goes with fibrous roots.

questions.text: Frogs and salamanders, which live both on land and in water, belong to the group called _____.
questions.explanation: Amphibians live partly on land and partly in water.

questions.text: Name three groups of plants based on their stem and height.
questions.explanation: Plants are grouped by height and stem hardness into herbs, shrubs, and trees.

questions.text: Give two examples of herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores.
questions.answer: Herbivores: cow, deer. Carnivores: lion, tiger. Omnivores: humans, crow.
questions.explanation: Standard examples for each food group.

questions.text: Why do scientists classify plants and animals?
questions.answer: Classification makes the huge variety of living things easier to study, identify, name, and conserve. It also helps us see relationships between species.
questions.explanation: Highlights the practical and scientific reasons for classification.

questions.text: How are leaves with parallel venation different from leaves with reticulate venation? Give an example of each.
questions.answer: Parallel venation has veins running side by side without crossing (e.g., grass, maize). Reticulate venation has veins forming a net-like pattern (e.g., mango, hibiscus).
questions.explanation: Highlights the visual and example difference between the two types.

questions.text: Look at the leaf of a peepal tree (parallel-like at first glance but actually reticulate) and the leaf of grass. How would you decide which is parallel and which is reticulate?
questions.answer: Trace the veins from the base of the leaf. If they run side by side without crossing, the venation is parallel (grass). If they branch and cross to form a net pattern, the venation is reticulate (peepal).
questions.explanation: Looks for an observation-based approach.

questions.text: How does a fish breathe in water?
questions.answer: A fish breathes through gills. Water enters the mouth, passes over the gills, and the gills extract dissolved oxygen from the water before the water flows out.
questions.explanation: Tests understanding of gill respiration.

questions.text: Compare a plant living in a desert with a plant living in a rainforest. Mention two differences in their adaptations.
questions.answer: A desert plant (like a cactus) has thick, fleshy stems to store water and spines instead of broad leaves to reduce water loss. A rainforest plant has broad leaves with drip tips to shed heavy rain and quickly absorb sunlight in the dim forest floor. The desert plant adapts to lack of water; the rainforest plant adapts to plenty of water and competition for light.
questions.explanation: Tests analytical comparison of adaptations.

questions.text: Why is conservation of biodiversity important?
questions.answer: Biodiversity supports food production, gives us medicines, keeps soil fertile, controls pests naturally, and keeps the environment balanced. Losing biodiversity affects human food, health, and well-being. Once a species is gone, it cannot be replaced.
questions.explanation: Tests evaluation and reasoning about conservation.

questions.text: Make a simple dichotomous key (yes/no questions) that would let a student tell apart these four animals: cow, eagle, fish, lizard.
questions.answer: Sample key. Q1: Does the animal live mostly in water? Yes -> Fish. No -> Q2. Q2: Does the animal have feathers? Yes -> Eagle. No -> Q3. Q3: Does the animal have hair/fur and feed milk to its young? Yes -> Cow. No -> Lizard. (Different but valid yes/no question paths are also acceptable.)
questions.explanation: Tests creating a dichotomous key — open-ended.

questions.text: You see a leaf with a net-like vein pattern. The plant most likely also has
questions.explanation: Reticulate venation typically goes with taproots and dicot seeds.

questions.text: Which is an example of an aquatic animal?
questions.explanation: Fish live in water — aquatic.

questions.text: Which is an example of an aerial animal (flying)?
questions.explanation: Birds fly — aerial.

questions.text: Microorganisms are
options: Living things too small to see with the eye
questions.answer: Living things too small to see with the eye
questions.explanation: Microorganisms (bacteria, amoeba) are tiny living organisms visible only under a microscope.

questions.text: Which is the BIGGEST group when classifying living things at the broadest level?
questions.explanation: At the broadest level, living things are split into plants, animals, and microorganisms.

questions.text: Which is a feature you can directly OBSERVE to classify a plant?
options: The shape of leaves and stem
questions.answer: The shape of leaves and stem
questions.explanation: Visible physical features like leaves and stem are observable; the others are not.

questions.text: Which animal is BEST adapted to a desert habitat?
questions.explanation: Camels conserve water and store fat in humps — desert adaptations.

questions.text: A plant that grows submerged in water has thin, ribbon-like leaves. This is most likely an adaptation for
questions.explanation: Thin leaves bend with water flow, avoiding tearing.

questions.text: Which step would BEST conserve biodiversity in a school garden?
options: Removing every insect we don't recognize
Planting many local species and avoiding chemical sprays
Keeping only one kind of plant
questions.answer: Planting many local species and avoiding chemical sprays
questions.explanation: Variety of native plants and reduced chemicals support biodiversity.

questions.text: Microorganisms are part of the diversity of life.
questions.explanation: Microorganisms are tiny living things and part of biodiversity.

questions.text: Cactus is well adapted to live in the desert.
questions.explanation: Cactus stores water in stems and has spines to reduce water loss — desert adaptation.

questions.text: All animals breathe through lungs.
questions.explanation: Fish breathe through gills, insects through tubes; not all animals use lungs.

questions.text: A peepal leaf has reticulate venation, so the peepal probably has a tap root.
questions.explanation: Reticulate venation usually pairs with taproot system.

questions.text: A bird that cannot fly is the _____.
questions.explanation: Ostrich is a flightless bird (also acceptable: penguin, emu).

questions.text: The desert animal known for its hump used to store fat is the _____.
questions.explanation: Camel's hump stores fat that the animal can break down for energy and water.

questions.text: A plant adapted to live in water is called an _____ plant.
questions.explanation: Aquatic plants live in water (e.g., water lily, hydrilla).

questions.text: Why is grouping organisms useful?
questions.answer: It makes a huge variety of living things easier to study, name, identify, compare, and conserve.
questions.explanation: Grouping creates order out of natural variety.

questions.text: You are given a coriander plant. List two features you would record to decide if it is a herb, shrub, or tree.
questions.answer: Height of the plant and hardness/colour of the stem. Coriander is short with a soft green stem, so it is a herb.
questions.explanation: Tests applying classification criteria to a real example.

questions.text: Compare adaptations of an aquatic animal (fish) and a terrestrial animal (cow) to their habitats.
questions.answer: A fish has a streamlined body, fins to swim, and gills to take oxygen from water. A cow has four legs to walk on land, lungs to breathe air, and is covered in hair to retain warmth. Each is built for the medium it lives in.
questions.explanation: Tests comparison across habitats.

questions.text: Imagine all bees disappear from your area. Discuss what changes you might see in plants, food, and other animals over time.
questions.answer: Without bees, many flowering plants would not be pollinated, so they would produce fewer fruits and seeds. Crops like apples, mangoes, and many vegetables would yield less, raising food prices. Animals that eat fruits and seeds (birds, monkeys) would have less food. Other plants that depend on the same pollinators might also decline. Over time the local environment would lose colour, food, and animal life. This shows that even one species — like bees — is connected to many others.
questions.explanation: Tests reasoning about interconnections in biodiversity.

questions.text: Which is NOT a microorganism?
questions.explanation: Lions are large mammals, not microorganisms.

questions.text: In a forest, the diversity of life means
options: many kinds of plants, animals, and microorganisms living together
questions.answer: many kinds of plants, animals, and microorganisms living together
questions.explanation: Forest biodiversity includes plants, animals, fungi, microorganisms.

questions.text: You collect a leaf with one main vein down the middle and many side veins forming a net. The plant is most likely a
questions.explanation: Reticulate venation is associated with dicots.

questions.text: Polar bears have white fur. The MOST scientific reason is
options: white fur blends with snow, helping them hunt and stay safe
questions.answer: white fur blends with snow, helping them hunt and stay safe
questions.explanation: Camouflage is an adaptation that aids survival.

questions.text: Which would have the BIGGEST positive effect on local biodiversity?
options: Protecting a wetland by stopping dumping of waste
questions.answer: Protecting a wetland by stopping dumping of waste
questions.explanation: Protecting a habitat preserves many species at once.

questions.text: Different students may use different valid features to classify the same set of plants.
questions.explanation: There are several valid ways to group; classifications depend on the chosen feature.

questions.text: Animals that live in cold places usually have less body fat than tropical animals.
questions.explanation: Cold-place animals usually have more fat (blubber) for insulation.

questions.text: Wheat is a _____ (monocot/dicot).
questions.explanation: Wheat seeds have a single cotyledon, making them monocots.

questions.text: Mango is a _____ (monocot/dicot).
questions.explanation: Mango seeds have two cotyledons, making them dicots.

questions.text: A plant with a single main thick root with smaller side branches has a _____ root system.
questions.explanation: Taproot is one main root with side branches.

questions.text: Mention any two ways an animal can be adapted to its habitat.
questions.answer: Sample answers: thick fur for cold habitats; webbed feet for swimming in water; long legs for running in open grasslands; sharp claws for climbing trees. Any two valid examples are correct.
questions.explanation: Tests understanding of adaptations.

questions.text: You are asked to group six animals: cow, sparrow, frog, fish, lizard, ant. Suggest two different ways to group them.
questions.answer: By habitat: land (cow, lizard, ant) — water (fish) — both (frog) — air (sparrow). By food: herbivore (cow), carnivore (sparrow, lizard), omnivore (frog, ant), aquatic (fish — varies). Any reasonable two-way grouping based on observable features is correct.
questions.explanation: Tests applying multiple grouping criteria.

questions.text: Suggest three actions a class of students can take to help protect biodiversity in their school surroundings.
questions.answer: Sample answers: (1) Plant native flowering plants to support local insects and birds. (2) Avoid using chemical pesticides; let natural pest controllers like ladybirds work. (3) Maintain a small water source like a bird bath. Any three reasonable actions accepted.
questions.explanation: Tests applying conservation knowledge to a school context.

questions.text: Design a small chart that classifies the following plants into herbs, shrubs, and trees: tulsi, rose, mango, neem, mint, hibiscus. For each, write the group it belongs to and ONE supporting feature you'd note.
questions.answer: Tulsi — herb (short, soft green stem). Rose — shrub (medium height, hard branching stem at base). Mango — tree (tall, thick woody stem). Neem — tree (tall, thick woody stem). Mint — herb (short, soft green stem). Hibiscus — shrub (medium height, hard branching stem). Chart format with columns 'Plant', 'Group', 'Feature' is acceptable.
questions.explanation: Tests creating a classification chart.
